solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: The fall of Kamala Harris?

blocks.note: surface reading: the politician's defeat, her downfall in the election
setter's reading: 'fall' is the American word for the season, and her election was held in November

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as political commentary on a downfall, but 'fall' is the US name for a season; the 2024 presidential election took place in early November.
explanation.definitionFit: Americans call the season between summer and winter the fall, so the British name for that season fits.

clue.text: A couple of females, clever and congenial

blocks.note: taken as written
F is the abbreviation for female, and a couple means two of them
an able person is capable or clever

explanation.surface: A pair of women are described as both bright and pleasant company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clever and congenial' looks like a pair of descriptions, but 'and' only joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone friendly, easy to talk to and pleasant in manner; they are close synonyms.

clue.text: Body temperature, approximately

blocks.note: T is the standard abbreviation for temperature
'or so' means roughly, approximately

explanation.surface: A rough estimate of someone's body temperature, as a nurse might give.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Body temperature' reads as one phrase, but 'Body' alone is the definition and the rest is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The trunk of a human figure, without head or limbs, is called the body, as in a sculpture's main mass.

clue.text: Stadium never condemned for accident

indicators.note: a condemned building is due for demolition, so these letters are knocked down and rebuilt in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A sports ground that was never declared unsafe is somehow the scene of an accident.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Condemned' sits naturally as a verb about the stadium, but it is the signal to rearrange the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A misadventure is an unlucky mishap; British coroners record 'death by misadventure' for accidental deaths.

clue.text: Fat Scottish landowner abandoning island

indicators.note: to abandon something is to leave it behind, so a letter is dropped from the word

blocks.note: a laird is the owner of a landed estate in Scotland
I is the abbreviation for island; this letter is removed

explanation.surface: An overweight Scottish laird leaves his island estate behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fat' looks like an adjective describing the landowner, but it is the definition, used as a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Lard is rendered pig fat used in cooking and baking, so it is a specific kind of the general substance.

clue.text: Generally free

blocks.note: first meaning: as a whole
second meaning: not captured, as of an escaped prisoner

explanation.walkthrough: The two words read as a single phrase meaning 'usually free of charge', but each is a separate meaning of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means 'in general, as a whole' and also describes a fugitive still on the loose and uncaptured.

clue.text: Doctor and I talk interminably

blocks.note: Dr is the abbreviation for doctor
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A patient complains that the doctor and they chat endlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: Treat 'I' as the Roman numeral, not the pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: To drone is to speak in a dull monotonous tone at tedious length, like the steady hum of a bee.

clue.text: Bishop worried about letter to Greek ambassador

indicators.note: 'about' can mean turned around, as in about-turn, so the word is flipped back to front

blocks.note: B is the chess notation for bishop
worried, in the sense of fretted or gnawed at, as in 'what's eating you?'

explanation.surface: A bishop frets over a letter he must send to the Greek ambassador.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on 'letter': not correspondence sent to a diplomat, but a character of the alphabet a Greek would use.
explanation.definitionFit: Beta is the second character of the Greek alphabet, so a letter belonging to a Greek diplomat's own script.

clue.text: Hit by a bullet? This will give you a boost

definitions.text: This will give you a boost

blocks.note: first meaning, literal: wounded by gunfire in a limb

blocks.clueFragment: This will give you a boost
blocks.note: second meaning, idiomatic: something that revives or encourages

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the first part is a literal reading of an idiom; the second part gives its everyday figurative sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom, from an injection of a stimulant, means a timely encouragement or boost, while literally it describes a gunshot wound.

clue.text: Anticipate enemies crossing river by middle of week

indicators.note: to cross something is to straddle it, so one piece spans around another
the centre of a word means only its central letters are kept

blocks.note: foes are enemies
R is the abbreviation for river
the two central letters of the four-letter word

explanation.surface: Expecting hostile forces to ford a river by midweek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' here means 'next to', placing the last piece beside the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: To foresee something is to predict or expect it before it happens, the same sense as anticipate.

clue.text: He’s going to love this magazine

blocks.note: 'he's going to' is 'he'll', written without the apostrophe
love is zero in tennis scoring, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A man predicts he will adore this particular magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: HELLO! is a British celebrity gossip magazine, full of photo spreads of famous people at home.
explanation.definitionFit: Hello! is the title of a well-known weekly celebrity publication in Britain, so the answer is an example.

clue.text: Programme made by bad actors abroad

indicators.note: abroad can mean astray or all over the place, so these letters are scattered into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A TV show filmed overseas by a cast of poor performers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abroad' seems to say where the filming happened, but it is the signal to rearrange the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadcast is a radio or television programme transmitted to the public, so the two nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Regret cruelty to an extent

indicators.note: only partly, so just a portion of the following word is used

blocks.note: the second to fourth letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone feels some remorse for having been cruel.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits at the start of 'cruelty' once its first letter is passed over.
explanation.definitionFit: To rue something is to wish it had not happened, an old-fashioned verb for feeling sorry about it.

clue.text: Times editor removed

blocks.note: eras are periods of history, times
ED is the abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: The editor of The Times newspaper has been sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' looks like the newspaper's name, but here it just means periods of history.
explanation.definitionFit: Something erased has been rubbed out or wiped away, which is one way of being taken out or deleted.

clue.text: Criminal married man who adored him?

definitions.note: the question mark flags that this is a playful description; the answer is the person who adores, of either sex

indicators.note: something criminal is wrong or crooked, so these letters are bent out of their order

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A wedded man commits a crime, perhaps for love of another man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal married man' reads as one description of a crook, but the first word is only the signal and the second is the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An admirer is a person who adores or looks up to someone, often a suitor with romantic feelings.

clue.text: A French team playing in Madrid? Amazing!

blocks.note: un is French for 'a'
Real Madrid is the famous Spanish football club

explanation.surface: A French side playing a match in Madrid, and the result is astonishing.
explanation.walkthrough: The football club is Real Madrid, so its team name supplies the second piece.
explanation.definitionFit: In slang, unreal is an exclamation of astonishment meaning incredible or too good to be true.

clue.text: Angela’s cooking an Italian dish

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so these letters are mixed into a new form

blocks.note: the name plus the S of the possessive, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Angela is in the kitchen making pasta for dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe S counts as a letter of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Lasagne is a baked pasta meal of layered sheets, meat sauce and cheese originating in Italy.

clue.text: Intend using Valium regularly

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every second letter is taken

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of the drug's name

explanation.surface: Someone plans to take a sedative on a regular basis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' seems to describe the drug habit, but it picks every other letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To aim to do something is to plan or mean to do it, a near synonym for intend.

clue.text: A chap who’s employed by the CIA?

definitions.note: describes a person, so it stands for the noun

blocks.note: taken as written
gent is short for gentleman, a chap

explanation.surface: Asking about the kind of man who works for American intelligence.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as one description, but 'A chap' is split off to build the answer and the rest describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: The CIA employs undercover operatives known as agents, so the answer is the job title of such a spy.

clue.text: After revolution, bosses attract attention

blocks.note: a revolution is one complete turn
heads are leaders or bosses

explanation.surface: After an uprising, the new leaders make sure they get noticed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolution' suggests a political uprising, but here it means a rotation.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that makes people look round at it is said to make heads swivel, an idiom for being noticed.

clue.text: Retiring English teacher getting pay increase

indicators.note: to retire is to go back, so the word runs backwards

blocks.note: pupils in British schools address a male teacher as sir
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: An English teacher about to retire receives a salary bump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English teacher' reads as a subject teacher, but the two words are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a rise is an increase in wages; Americans call it a raise.

clue.text: Adventurous girl caught in a lie

indicators.note: one thing being inside another means it is placed within it

blocks.note: taken as written
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A daring young woman is caught out telling a fib.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adventurous girl' points to Lewis Carroll's heroine of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of Carroll's book has adventures in Wonderland, so she is the best-known adventurous girl in fiction.

clue.text: Panic after leader’s departure? That’s a mistake

indicators.note: once the one at the front has left, the opening letter is gone

blocks.note: terror is extreme fear or panic

explanation.surface: Panicking once the boss has quit would be a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leader' suggests a political leader, but it is the first letter of the word for panic.
explanation.definitionFit: An error is a wrong action or a slip, the same as a mistake; the two words are ordinary synonyms.

clue.text: Moderate South Africa group holding power

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: SA is the abbreviation for South Africa
P is the physics symbol for power
a ring is a group of people, such as a spy ring

explanation.surface: A moderate South African political group that holds power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moderate' looks like an adjective describing the group, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sparing means using only a little, economical and restrained, which is a moderate amount rather than excess.

clue.text: Attempt to arrest old right-winger

indicators.note: to arrest someone is to take them into custody, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: a try is an attempt
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: An attempt is made to arrest an elderly right-wing politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old right-winger' reads as one phrase, but 'old' is a piece of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative Party, the main party on the political right.

clue.text: Limped excessively carrying hamper

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it within, so the letters sit inside the words before

blocks.note: found running across the two words

explanation.surface: Someone limped badly, weighed down by a picnic basket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hamper' suggests a wicker basket, but it is the verb meaning hinder.
explanation.definitionFit: To hamper someone is to hinder or obstruct their progress, which is what impeding means.
